title: Employee Data Use: One in Five Trust Leaders a Great Deal
author: Gallup
summary: This Gallup analysis reports that only one in five employees who work on a device have a great deal of trust in their leaders to use employee data responsibly. Trust is tightly linked to engagement: 40% of engaged employees have great trust compared with 4% of actively disengaged employees. Employees often lack clear information about what is collected, and just 19% say anyone has spoken with them about it. They are more comfortable with constructive uses, such as supporting team effectiveness and development, than with uses that affect evaluations, staffing or scheduling. Direct conversations about data are linked to higher trust, and managers with greater visibility into data practices report more trust. Gallup concludes that transparency about purpose and use, and equipping managers to explain it, supports trust in leadership.
points: Only 20% of employees have a great deal of trust that leaders will use employee data responsibly.
Trust tracks engagement closely, from 40% among engaged employees to 4% among those actively disengaged.
Communication is thin, with only 19% of employees saying someone has talked with them about the data collected on their work.
Employees accept data used to support development and team effectiveness more readily than data used in reviews, staffing or scheduling.
Managers with direct data access are far more trusting, so giving them visibility helps them answer employee questions.
quotes: One in five employees who work on a computer or another device regularly have “a great deal” of trust in their organization’s leaders to use employee data responsibly.

Forty percent of engaged employees have a great deal of trust in leaders to use employee data responsibly, compared with 13% of employees who are not engaged and just 4% of those who are actively disengaged.
Direct communication is uncommon: 19% of all employees say someone at work has spoken with them about data or metrics their organization collects about their work.
They are more comfortable when they see a constructive purpose and clear benefit and less comfortable when data could affect evaluations or other decisions about their work.
Open communication can help employees understand what data their organization collects, how it uses those data and what limits it places on their use.
Organizations that give managers appropriate visibility into their data practices can better equip them to answer employee questions
Across all potential uses, employees are more comfortable with their employer using data about their activity than data about the content of their activity.
